summary: Redefines the format of message bodies to let multi-part, textual and non-textual content be represented and exchanged without loss of information. This was the original MIME specification, and it was replaced by RFC 1521.

plainLanguage.summary: MIME gives an email body a structure. Each part says what it contains, what character set it uses and how it was encoded for the trip, so a picture, a sound clip and a paragraph of Japanese text can travel in the same message and arrive intact.

questions: what are the mime content types
subtitle: How an email body can carry several kinds of content, in any character set, without losing anything.

tldr.problem: RFC 822 mail bodies are flat ASCII text. There is no way to put an image, a sound file or text in a non-Latin character set into one without losing information.
tldr.mechanism: MIME adds four header fields: MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, and the optional Content-ID and Content-Description. A multipart body holds several parts, each preceded by a boundary line, and each part can have its own type and encoding.
tldr.outcome: Mail can now carry text in many character sets, formatted text, images, audio, video and whole messages, while old readers still see something sensible. The document has been replaced by RFC 1521.

facts.label: Boundary length limit
facts.value: 70 characters, not counting the two leading hyphens

today: RFC 1341 was a Proposed Standard published in June 1992. It has been obsoleted by RFC 1521, which is the current MIME specification for the format of Internet message bodies.

sections.title: Why MIME Was Needed
sections.content:
RFC 822 defines a message representation protocol which specifies considerable detail about message headers, but which leaves the message content, or message body, as flat ASCII text. This document redefines the format of message bodies to allow multi-part textual and non-textual message bodies to be represented and exchanged without loss of information. Because RFC 822 said so little about message bodies, this document is largely orthogonal to, rather than a revision of, RFC 822.

The limitations of RFC 822 mail become apparent when gateways are designed to exchange mail between RFC 822 hosts and X.400 hosts. X.400 specifies mechanisms for the inclusion of non-textual body parts. The current standards for mapping X.400 messages to RFC 822 messages specify that either X.400 non-textual body parts should be converted to an ASCII format, or that they should be discarded, notifying the RFC 822 user that discarding has occurred. That is clearly undesirable, as information a user may wish to receive is lost. Even though a user's mail agent may not have the capability of dealing with the non-textual body part, the user might have some mechanism external to the agent that can extract useful information from it.

The document describes several mechanisms that combine to solve most of these problems without introducing serious incompatibilities. The design goal was explicitly to include multiple objects in a single message, to represent body text in character sets other than US-ASCII, to represent formatted multi-font text messages, to represent non-textual material such as images and audio fragments, and to facilitate later extensions defining new types of Internet mail for use by cooperating mail agents. It does not extend Internet mail header fields to permit anything other than US-ASCII text data, which is the subject of a companion document.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain text mail could not carry a picture or an Asian-language message without throwing something away. MIME fixes that by describing what each part of a body is and how it was encoded.

sections.title: The Content-Type Header Field
sections.content:
The purpose of the Content-Type field is to describe the data contained in the body fully enough that the receiving user agent can pick an appropriate mechanism to present the data to the user. The field gives a type and a subtype identifier, followed by a set of parameters in an attribute/value notation. The ordering of parameters is not significant, and among the defined parameters is a charset parameter by which the character set used in the body may be declared.

The top-level Content-Type declares the general type of data, while the subtype specifies a specific format for that type. A Content-Type of image/xyz is enough to tell a user agent that the data is an image, even if it has no knowledge of the specific image format. An initial set of seven top-level Content-Types is defined: text, multipart, application, message, image, audio and video. That set is intended to be substantially complete, and additions to the larger set of supported types are expected to grow over time, with new values registered through IANA.

Two further optional header fields may be used to describe the data in a message body: Content-ID, which identifies the body, and Content-Description, which carries a human-readable description of it. The default character set, which must be assumed in the absence of a charset parameter, is US-ASCII, and it is strongly recommended that new user agents explicitly specify a character set. The default Content-Type for Internet mail, text/plain; charset=us-ascii, describes existing practice, the body type defined by RFC 822.

MIME has been carefully designed as an extensible mechanism, and the set of content-type and subtype pairs and their associated parameters is expected to grow significantly with time.
sections.plainLanguage: The Content-Type header says what the body is: a broad type such as text or image, and a narrower subtype such as plain or jpeg. Parameters add detail, such as which character set a text part uses.

sections.title: Content-Transfer-Encoding
sections.content:
Many Content-Types which could usefully be transported via email are represented, in their natural format, as 8-bit character or binary data. Such data cannot be transmitted over some transport protocols: RFC 821 restricts mail messages to 7-bit US-ASCII data with 1000 character lines. It is therefore necessary to define a standard mechanism for re-encoding such data into a 7-bit short-line format, and this document specifies that such encodings will be indicated by a new Content-Transfer-Encoding header field. The field's value is one of BASE64, QUOTED-PRINTABLE, 8BIT, 7BIT, BINARY, or an x-token, and the values are not case sensitive.

An encoding type of 7BIT requires that the body is already in a seven-bit mail-ready representation, and it is the default value assumed if the Content-Transfer-Encoding header field is not present. The values 8bit, 7bit and binary all imply that no encoding has been performed, but they are useful as indications of the kind of data contained, and therefore of the kind of encoding that might be needed for transmission in a given transport system.

Two mechanisms are defined. Quoted-Printable represents data that largely consists of printable ASCII characters, so the encoded form remains largely recognizable by humans, and is useful for text that is mostly but not entirely 7-bit. Base64 represents arbitrary sequences of octets in a form that is not humanly readable, using a 65-character subset of US-ASCII so that 6 bits are represented per printable character, and the encoded data are consistently only about 33 percent larger than the unencoded data. The encoding process represents 24-bit groups of input bits as output strings of 4 encoded characters, and the output must be represented in lines of no more than 76 characters each.

Only the bit-width tokens are permitted for an entity of type multipart or message, so that data is never encoded more than once. The creation of new Content-Transfer-Encoding values is explicitly and strongly discouraged, and their use is allowed only as the result of an agreement between cooperating user agents.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail transport can only carry seven-bit text, so bodies are rewritten before sending and decoded on arrival. Quoted-printable keeps text readable; base64 packs any bytes into text at the cost of about a third more volume.

sections.title: Multipart Bodies and Their Boundaries
sections.content:
In the case of multiple part messages, in which one or more different sets of data are combined in a single body, a multipart Content-Type field must appear in the entity's header. The body must then contain one or more body parts, each preceded by an encapsulation boundary, and the last one followed by a closing boundary. Each part starts with an encapsulation boundary, and then contains a body part consisting of a header area, a blank line and a body area. A body part is similar to an RFC 822 message in syntax, but different in meaning: no header fields are actually required in body parts, and the only header fields with defined meaning are those whose names begin with Content-.

All subtypes of the multipart type share a common syntax, so that all conformant user agents will at least be able to recognize and separate the parts of any multipart entity, even of an unrecognized subtype. The Content-Type field for multipart entities requires one parameter, boundary, which is used to specify the encapsulation boundary. The encapsulation boundary is a line consisting entirely of two hyphen characters followed by the boundary parameter value. The encapsulation boundary must not appear inside any of the encapsulated parts, so it is crucial that the composing agent can choose and specify a unique boundary. Encapsulation boundaries must be no longer than 70 characters, not counting the two leading hyphens.

The boundary must occur at the beginning of a line, and the initial CRLF is considered to be part of the encapsulation boundary rather than part of the preceding part. The boundary must be followed immediately either by another CRLF and the header fields for the next part, or by two CRLFs, in which case there are no header fields for the next part and it is assumed to be of Content-Type text/plain. The encapsulation boundary following the last body part is a distinguished delimiter with two more hyphens added at the end of the line. Text before the first boundary and after the last one is the preamble and the epilogue, and should generally be left blank.
sections.plainLanguage: A multipart body is a list of parts separated by lines beginning with two hyphens. Each part has its own headers and its own body, and the sender must pick a separator that cannot occur inside the content.

sections.title: The Multipart Subtypes
sections.content:
The primary subtype for multipart, mixed, is intended for use when the body parts are independent and intended to be displayed serially. Any multipart subtype that an implementation does not recognize should be treated as being of subtype mixed.

The multipart/alternative type is syntactically identical to multipart/mixed, but the semantics are different: each of the parts is an alternative version of the same information. User agents should recognize that the content of the various parts are interchangeable, and should either choose the best type based on the user's environment and preferences, or offer the user the available alternatives. In general, choosing the best type means displaying only the last part that can be displayed. User agents that compose multipart/alternative entities should place the body parts in increasing order of preference, with the preferred format last, so for fancy text the plainest format comes first and the richest format last. Receiving agents should pick and display the last format they are capable of displaying. What is most critical is that the user not automatically be shown multiple versions of the same data: either the user should be shown the last recognized version, or should explicitly be given the choice.

Two further subtypes are defined. The multipart/digest subtype is for the special case in which all the parts are messages. The multipart/parallel subtype is intended for parts that are to be displayed side by side, and its parts are typically of type message or multipart.
sections.plainLanguage: multipart/mixed is a list of unrelated parts. multipart/alternative is the same message in several formats, with the richest last. multipart/digest holds whole messages, and multipart/parallel holds parts meant to be shown together.

sections.title: Minimal MIME Conformance
sections.content:
The mechanisms described in the document are open-ended, and it is not expected that all implementations will support all of the Content-Types described. Appendix A defines a basic applicability statement for a subset of them, which defines a minimal level of conformance that allows useful interworking of messages with content that differs from US-ASCII text.

A mail user agent that is MIME-conformant must always generate a MIME-Version: 1.0 header field. It must recognize the Content-Transfer-Encoding header field and decode all received data encoded with either the quoted-printable or base64 implementations, and encode any data sent that is not in seven-bit mail-ready representation using one of these transformations and include the appropriate header field. It must recognize and interpret the Content-Type header field and avoid showing users raw data with a Content-Type field other than text, and be able to send at least text/plain messages with the character set specified as a parameter if it is not US-ASCII.

For text it must recognize and display text mail with the character set US-ASCII, recognize other character sets at least to the extent of telling the user which one is used, and recognize the ISO-8859-* character sets well enough to display the characters common to ISO-8859-* and US-ASCII. For message it must recognize and display at least the primary encapsulation. For multipart it must recognize the mixed subtype and display the message-level and body-part-level headers and then each body part individually, recognize the alternative subtype and avoid showing the user redundant parts, and treat any unrecognized subtype as if it were mixed. For application it must offer the ability to remove either of the two transfer encodings and put the result in a user file.

Upon encountering any unrecognized Content-Type, an implementation must treat it as if it had a Content-Type of application/octet-stream with no parameters. The meaning of MIME-conformance is that it is safe to send virtually any kind of properly marked data to users of such mail systems, because they will at least be able to treat the data as undifferentiated binary.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets a floor: a conformant mail program must handle the two encodings, must understand text, message and multipart, and must treat anything it does not recognise as an opaque file rather than dumping it on the screen.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN TOP-LEVEL MIME CONTENT TYPES

items.title: text
items.text: Textual information in a number of character sets and formatted text description languages.

items.title: multipart
items.text: Several body parts, possibly of differing types, combined into one message.

items.title: application
items.text: Application data or binary data, and hence an electronic mail file transfer service.

items.title: image
items.text: Still image, that is picture, data.

items.title: video
items.text: Video or moving image data, possibly with audio as part of the composite video data format.

cells: Data that is mostly printable ASCII
A 65-character subset of US-ASCII, 6 bits per character
No more than 76 characters per line

viz.caption: THE TWO-PART MULTIPART EXAMPLE FROM RFC 1341

data.title: A multipart/mixed message
data.code:
From: Nathaniel Borenstein <nsb@bellcore.com>
To:  Ned Freed <ned@innosoft.com>
Subject: Sample message
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-type: multipart/mixed; boundary="simple boundary"

This is the preamble.  It is to be ignored.
--simple boundary

This is implicitly typed plain ASCII text.
It does NOT end with a linebreak.
--simple boundary
Content-type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii

This is explicitly typed plain ASCII text.
It DOES end with a linebreak.

--simple boundary--
This is the epilogue.  It is also to be ignored.
